title: White Lines on Your KDP Cover? Here's Why It Happens
description: Seeing thin white lines or borders on your printed KDP cover? Learn how bleed, trim tolerance, borders, and Canva exports cause white edges — and how to fix them correctly.

shortAnswer: White lines on a KDP cover are caused by insufficient bleed, borders placed too close to the trim edge, Canva export alignment errors, or normal trim tolerance shifting the cut slightly outside the printed area. Extend backgrounds into bleed, remove risky edge borders, and export using the correct PDF Print settings to fix the issue.

faqs.question: Why do white lines appear on my printed KDP cover?
faqs.answer: White lines appear when the background or artwork stops exactly at the trim edge and the physical cut shifts slightly outward. Even a fraction of a millimeter can expose blank white paper beside the printed color.

faqs.question: Does KDP trim books differently every time?
faqs.answer: Not dramatically, but small variation is normal in industrial printing. KDP trims within an accepted tolerance range. Bleed and safe margins are designed specifically to absorb that natural variation.

faqs.question: How much bleed should I use for KDP?
faqs.answer: KDP requires 0.125 inches (approximately 3.2mm) of bleed on outside edges. Your background and edge artwork should extend fully to that bleed boundary, not just to the trim line.

faqs.question: Are borders dangerous on KDP covers?
faqs.answer: Yes, especially thin borders placed within 0.125 inches of the trim edge. Any trim shift makes the border look uneven — thicker on one side, thinner on another — even when the PDF was perfectly centered.

faqs.question: Why did my Canva design look correct but print with white edges?
faqs.answer: Canva's canvas view shows the design at trim size. If the background was not dragged past the bleed guide, or if the project was exported without bleed enabled, the printed file has no spare artwork to absorb trim movement.

faqs.question: Can trim shifts expose white edges even with bleed enabled?
faqs.answer: Yes, if bleed is enabled in KDP settings but the background does not actually extend into the bleed area in the PDF. Enabling bleed in the KDP project does not automatically extend your artwork — the source file must do that.

faqs.question: Should my background extend past the bleed line?
faqs.answer: Yes. Your background should extend all the way to the bleed boundary. Stopping at the trim line is not sufficient. Bleed exists precisely to give the cutter printed artwork to pass through.

faqs.question: Why does my spine seam look visible after printing?
faqs.answer: Spine seams become visible when wraparound backgrounds do not align perfectly or when the spine is very thin. Thin spines have less tolerance for artwork misalignment. Keep non-essential artwork simple in the spine region.

faqs.question: Can KDP Previewer miss print issues?
faqs.answer: Yes. KDP Previewer renders a digital interpretation of your file. It cannot simulate physical trim shift. A cover that looks perfect in Previewer can still show white lines after physical production.

faqs.question: Is a white edge on my proof copy a KDP defect or my file?
faqs.answer: In most cases it is the file. White lines caused by trim tolerance are a normal production outcome when bleed is missing or insufficient. KDP's production is not defective — the file simply did not include the buffer required for physical printing.

summary: White lines on KDP covers are almost always caused by missing bleed, borders too close to trim, or backgrounds that stop at the trim line instead of extending past it.
KDP printing has a natural trim tolerance. Your design must account for that movement with proper bleed and safe margins.
Canva designs can look correct on screen while missing the bleed extension that physical printing requires. Always verify PDF dimensions and use PDF Print export.

content:
You ordered a proof copy. The file looked perfect on screen — centered artwork, clean edges, sharp text. Then the physical book arrived and there are thin white lines along the cover edge, or a pale seam near the spine, or one side looks like it has a white border the design never called for.

This is one of the most common KDP print-production problems, and it is almost always preventable. The design is not broken. The printer is not malfunctioning. The issue is almost always a gap between what the file delivers digitally and what industrial printing requires physically.

White lines on a KDP cover are usually caused by one or more of these things: insufficient bleed, a background that stops at the trim line instead of extending past it, borders placed too close to the edge, Canva export settings that omit bleed, or a misunderstanding of how physical trim tolerance works. This guide explains every cause in plain language — and gives you specific, production-tested fixes.

## Why White Lines Appear on Printed KDP Covers

Amazon KDP prints books on industrial presses and then trims them to the final size. That trimming step is not a pixel-perfect digital operation. It is a physical blade cutting through a stack of paper. The blade has a small accepted range of movement called trim tolerance.

KDP's trim tolerance is typically within a few millimeters of the target cut line. Under normal production conditions, a cover might trim a fraction of a millimeter to the left, right, top, or bottom of the intended edge. That movement is considered acceptable in commercial print production.

The problem happens when a cover background or artwork stops exactly at the trim line with no extra buffer. If the cut moves slightly outward, the blade exits the printed area and lands on blank white paper. That unprinted strip becomes the white line you see on the finished book.

What looks perfectly centered on screen is not immune. A digital preview shows a rectangle. Physical printing produces an object with real-world manufacturing tolerances. Those are different things, and professional print files account for that difference using bleed.

Bleed is extra printed artwork that extends beyond the trim line. The KDP standard bleed is 0.125 inches on each outside edge. That extra artwork is cut away during production, but while it exists it gives the blade something printed to cut through even if the cut shifts slightly.

Without that buffer, the file is relying on the cut landing exactly at the pixel boundary between printed artwork and blank paper — every single time, on every copy. In reality, it will not.

## The Most Common Causes of White Lines on KDP Covers

### Backgrounds Not Extending Far Enough

The most frequent cause of white lines is a background that stops at the trim line rather than extending into bleed. This happens because the trim line is often the visible edge of the canvas in Canva, Photoshop, Illustrator, or Affinity. Designers naturally fill the visible canvas and assume that is enough.

It is not enough. The background must continue 0.125 inches past the trim line on every outside edge. That extra area is the bleed. It is printed, then cut away. Its only job is to make sure the final edge has solid color even if the blade moves slightly.

A black cover, a dark gradient, a photo background, or any edge-to-edge texture that stops at the trim edge is vulnerable. The thinner the background stops short, the more likely any trim shift will expose white paper. On a full-black cover this becomes very obvious: white paper against black ink creates a high-contrast line that the eye notices immediately.

For a deeper explanation of why background extension matters at the production level, see the [background colors must extend past trim size guide](/blog/why-background-colors-must-extend-past-trim-size).

### Borders Too Close to the Edge

Thin borders near the cover edge are one of the most reliable ways to make trim tolerance visible. A border acts like a ruler. It is a straight line at a specific distance from the edge. When the physical trim shifts even slightly, that straight line no longer sits at the same distance from the edge on all four sides. One side looks closer, another looks farther. The symmetry breaks visibly.

This is not a KDP defect. It is a design decision that makes normal production variation obvious. A cover with a 1-point white border placed 0.1 inches from the edge will frequently show uneven borders in the printed proof — not because printing is bad, but because the design has no tolerance for movement.

The safer approach is to move borders inward — at minimum 0.25 inches from the trim edge, ideally further. Better still, rethink whether a tight border is necessary at all. Full bleed designs without thin edge frames are inherently more forgiving because there is no ruler-like reference line for the eye to measure against.

Canva users often create these borders by drawing a rectangle near the canvas edge or by using a frame template that places a border at or near the trim. Those borders may look polished in the preview but will reliably expose trim variation in print.

### Incorrect Bleed Setup

Bleed has two separate components that must both be correct: the KDP project setting and the actual artwork in the file.

Setting KDP to bleed without extending the artwork achieves nothing. The project expects bleed, but the background still stops at trim. The result is identical to having no bleed at all.

Exporting from Canva with bleed disabled sends a PDF at trim size rather than bleed size. The PDF is missing the 0.125 inches of extra artwork on each side. Even if the Canva canvas was built correctly, the exported PDF carries no bleed.

A mismatch between the cover bleed setting and the interior bleed setting can also create confusion in KDP Previewer. If those do not agree, the upload can flag dimension errors. The [interior and cover file mismatch guide](/blog/interior-and-cover-file-dont-match-kdp) covers that specific overlap.

The practical check: after exporting, open the PDF and verify the page dimensions. A 6 x 9 cover with proper bleed should be larger than 6 x 9. If the exported cover PDF is exactly 6 x 9, bleed is missing from the file regardless of what the project settings say.

### Canva Export Alignment Problems

Canva is widely used for KDP covers, and it handles bleed correctly when used correctly. The problem is that Canva hides misalignment well. A background rectangle that visually fills the canvas may actually stop at the trim edge rather than the bleed boundary. The bleed area in Canva is outside the visible canvas border and is only revealed when bleed view is turned on.

Canva also uses element snapping, which tends to snap objects to the canvas edge rather than the bleed boundary. A designer who drags a background to the edge and sees it snap into place has likely snapped it to trim, not to bleed.

When exporting, the correct settings are PDF Print, with bleed marks and crop marks turned off, and dimensions verified against the KDP template. Standard PDF export from Canva often strips bleed entirely. Exporting without enabling PDF Print is a common reason why a Canva cover arrives at trim size with no bleed.

Another Canva issue is scaling. If you built a design for one trim size and then resized the canvas for a different trim size, element positions relative to the bleed guide may shift. Always verify the bleed after any resize.

### Spine Misalignment and Wraparound Issues

For paperbacks, the cover is a full wrap: front cover, spine, and back cover in a single file. When a background wraps around all three panels, the color must flow continuously across the full width. If the background calculation is slightly off, a seam can appear at the spine fold.

Spine width is determined by page count, paper type, and trim size. If the spine width in the design does not match KDP's calculated spine width for the final book, the spine artwork will be in the wrong position. The wraparound background may have a gap, a line, or an exposed strip at the fold.

Thin spines — books under roughly 100 pages — are especially vulnerable because there is very little margin for alignment error. A 2mm shift on a 4mm spine is a 50% position error.

For spine-specific alignment problems and how to calculate the correct spine width, see the [KDP spine text off-center guide](/blog/fix-kdp-spine-text-off-center).

## How Much Bleed You Actually Need

KDP's required bleed is 0.125 inches (3.2mm) on each outside edge that needs bleed. For a full-wrap paperback cover, that means 0.125 inches outside the left edge of the back cover, 0.125 inches above the top edge, and 0.125 inches below the bottom edge, and 0.125 inches outside the right edge of the front cover.

The spine edge is not a bleed edge — the spine sits between the front and back panels, not at the outside trim. The fold lines at the spine are production boundaries, not cut lines.

The 0.125 inches is a minimum. It is the amount the printer expects. But when designing edge-to-edge backgrounds, thinking only about that minimum can create a second problem: artwork that visually looks like it is barely clinging to the edge even after the bleed is technically correct.

For designs with strong edge-to-edge intent, extending backgrounds 0.15 to 0.2 inches provides additional visual safety. For designs with organic or textured backgrounds — gradients, bokeh, rough textures — the extra extension costs nothing and adds real print protection.

Safe area is the opposite direction. Text, logos, author names, titles, and subtitles should stay at least 0.25 inches inside the trim line. Some designers push this to 0.375 inches for added safety. Content in the outer 0.25 inches of a cover is at risk of appearing cramped, being visually cut off, or producing inconsistent spacing across copies.

The three zones to always visualize are:

- **Bleed zone:** 0.125 inches outside trim — background extends here, nothing else
- **Trim line:** the intended final cut edge
- **Safe zone:** 0.25 inches or more inside trim — all important content stays here

## Step-by-Step Fixes That Actually Work

### Extend Backgrounds Beyond the Bleed

The most direct fix for white edge problems is to extend the background past the trim line into the full bleed area. Do not stop at the trim. Do not stop partway into bleed. The background should reach the outer bleed boundary on every outside edge.

In Canva: turn on bleed view (under File > Show Print Bleed), then drag the background element past the pink bleed guide on all sides. Check that each corner is fully covered. Export as PDF Print with bleed.

In Photoshop or Affinity: if the document was set up with bleed, extend the background layer to the bleed boundary using the canvas guides. If the document was set up at trim size only, the cleanest fix is to rebuild the file at the correct bleed-inclusive dimensions.

In Illustrator: expand the background rectangle beyond the artboard edge into the defined bleed area. Use the bleed guides in the print dialog to verify extension before export.

For photo backgrounds: resizing the photo to extend into bleed may crop part of the image. If the photo has a subject near the edge, check that the subject remains inside the safe zone after the photo is extended.

### Remove or Reposition Thin Borders Near the Edge

If the white line is appearing alongside a border or frame, the fastest fix is to remove the border entirely or move it significantly inward.

Any border within 0.2 inches of the trim edge is a risk. Any border within 0.1 inches of the trim edge will almost certainly look uneven in print. The border does not need to disappear from the design — it needs to move far enough inward that normal trim variation cannot make it look asymmetric.

Alternatives to edge borders that still create a finished, framed look:

- A design element 0.375 inches or more from the edge
- A color band or texture band that wraps into bleed rather than acting as a frame
- A vignette or gradient that softens naturally toward the edge rather than defining it
- No border at all, with a strong typographic hierarchy doing the visual framing

### Rebuild the Cover Using Proper Safe Margins

If the current cover has multiple elements that are too close to the edge, rebuilding the spacing is more efficient than individually adjusting each element.

Start from the KDP template for your trim size and page count. That template provides accurate bleed, trim, and safe area guides. Use those guides as your layout boundaries, not the raw canvas edge.

Recommended minimum distances from the trim line:

- Title: 0.375 inches inward from trim
- Author name: 0.375 inches inward from trim
- Subtitle: 0.375 inches inward from trim
- Logo or publisher mark: 0.375 inches inward from trim
- Any decorative border: 0.25 inches minimum, 0.375 recommended

The safe area is not just a printing requirement — it also improves the visual design. Content that crowds the edge looks uncomfortable even in digital thumbnails. Giving important elements breathing room improves readability and makes the cover feel more professional.

### Export Correctly from Canva

The most common Canva mistake that causes white lines is a wrong export. The correct workflow:

1. Set the document size to match the KDP full-wrap cover dimensions, including bleed — not just the trim size.
2. Turn on bleed view (File > Show Print Bleed) before finalizing the design.
3. Drag all backgrounds past the pink bleed guide on every outside edge.
4. Keep all text, logos, and important art inside the safe area.
5. When ready to export: click Share > Download > PDF Print.
6. Make sure **Crop marks and bleed** is checked. This includes bleed in the PDF.
7. Do not add extra crop marks unless KDP specifically requires them for your workflow — KDP generally does not.
8. Open the exported PDF and verify the page dimensions match the expected bleed-inclusive size.

Common Canva mistakes to avoid: exporting as Standard PDF instead of PDF Print; unchecking the bleed option in export; building the design at trim size then assuming bleed is handled automatically; using a template that was not designed for KDP print specifications.

### Use KDP Previewer Correctly

KDP Previewer is an important step but it has real limitations. Previewer renders a digital simulation of your file. It cannot simulate physical trim shift. A cover that passes Previewer without any warnings can still print with white lines if the bleed extension is insufficient.

What Previewer does catch: content outside the printable area, text in the barcode zone, dimension mismatches between cover and interior, gross bleed omissions.

What Previewer does not catch: fine trim shift scenarios, borderline bleed extension that technically passes but offers no production safety margin, Canva alignment errors that look correct at screen resolution.

The practical advice: use Previewer as a minimum check, not a final guarantee. After Previewer passes, order a physical proof copy before approving wide distribution. The proof copy is the only way to see what the physical trim actually produces on your specific cover design.

If the Previewer shows the cover looking cropped, shifted, or with unexpected white areas before you even reach the physical proof stage, compare the file against the [cropped KDP cover guide](/blog/kdp-cover-uploaded-successfully-but-looks-cropped).

## Real Example: Why a Perfect Canva Cover Printed with White Edges

Here is a realistic scenario that illustrates every cause discussed in this article.

A designer creates a paperback cover in Canva. The design uses a full black background, a white title, and a thin white rectangular border placed about 0.08 inches from the edge of the canvas. The canvas size is set to the trim size of the finished book, not the bleed-inclusive size. The designer exports using Standard PDF.

The Canva preview looks clean. The KDP Previewer shows the cover without warnings. The designer approves and orders a proof copy.

The physical proof arrives with two problems: a thin white line along the right edge of the front cover, and the white border looks slightly thicker on the bottom than the top.

What happened: The background was a black rectangle that filled the trim-size canvas. Because the canvas was set to trim size and the export used Standard PDF, the PDF had no bleed extension. The physical trim shifted 1.5mm to the right of the intended cut line. That exposed 1.5mm of blank white paper beside the black background — the white line.

The border problem happened because the same 1.5mm trim shift moved the relationship between the cut edge and the thin white frame. The frame was 0.08 inches from the edge. After the cut shifted, the frame was 0.02 inches from the top edge and 0.12 inches from the bottom edge. The border looked visually uneven even though the PDF was centered.

The fix involved three changes. First, the canvas was rebuilt at the bleed-inclusive size, and the black background was extended into full bleed on all four outside edges. Second, the thin border was removed and replaced with a subtle vignette effect applied to the inner portion of the background — well inside the safe area. Third, the export was changed to PDF Print with bleed enabled. The revised proof copy came back with no white lines and visually consistent edges.

## Cover Design Styles Most Likely to Cause White Lines

Some design choices are inherently higher risk for white line problems:

**Ultra-thin edge borders.** Any border thinner than 2 points placed within 0.2 inches of the trim is a trim tolerance recorder. It will make every small cut variation visible.

**Perfectly symmetrical frames.** A four-sided frame at equal distance from all edges gives the eye a reference ruler. Trim variation in any direction breaks the symmetry noticeably.

**Edge-hugging artwork with hard stops.** Artwork that ends with a sharp color boundary exactly at or near the trim — a solid rectangle, a hard-edged photo crop, a geometric shape — exposes trim shift the moment the cut moves.

**Hard-stop backgrounds.** A background color that transitions to white at the trim edge with no extension is always at risk. The white paper behind it is the white line waiting to happen.

Safer design choices for print production:

**Full bleed textures and organic backgrounds.** A textured gradient or natural photography background that extends into bleed and fades organically toward the edge gives the printer room and does not define hard reference lines near trim.

**Oversized imagery.** A photo background that extends generously past trim on all sides provides bleed naturally and gives the print process ample printed material to cut through.

**No edge borders, or widely inset frames.** A design that uses typographic hierarchy and color blocking rather than tight edge framing has no ruler-like elements for trim shift to break.

## FAQ

### Why do white lines appear on my printed KDP cover?

White lines appear when the background or artwork stops at the trim line and the physical cut shifts slightly outward, exposing blank white paper. Adding the correct bleed extension prevents this.

### Does KDP trim books differently every time?

Small variation is normal in industrial trimming. KDP operates within an accepted tolerance range. Bleed and safe margins absorb that variation so it does not affect print quality.

### How much bleed should I use for KDP?

KDP requires 0.125 inches (3.2mm) of bleed on each outside edge. All background artwork should extend to that boundary. Safe-area content should sit at least 0.25 inches inside the trim line.

### Are borders dangerous on KDP covers?

Thin borders near the edge act as trim tolerance recorders. Normal cutting variation makes them look uneven. Move borders at least 0.25 inches inward, or use safer design alternatives.

### Why did my Canva design look correct but print with white edges?

Canva's canvas view shows the design at trim size. If the background was not extended past the bleed guide, or if the file was exported as Standard PDF rather than PDF Print with bleed, the physical print file has no bleed buffer.

### Can trim shifts expose white edges even with bleed enabled in KDP?

Yes. Enabling bleed in KDP settings does not extend your artwork. The background in the actual PDF must reach the bleed boundary. Always verify PDF dimensions after export.

### Should my background extend past the bleed line?

Yes. The background should extend all the way to the bleed boundary — not to the trim line. The bleed area is printed and cut away, but while it exists it protects the final edge.

### Why does my spine seam look visible after printing?

Spine seams appear when the spine width in the design does not match KDP's calculated spine width, or when the background is not continuous across the full wrap. Thin spines are more vulnerable.

### Can KDP Previewer miss print issues?

Yes. Previewer is a digital simulation. It cannot predict physical trim shift. A cover that passes Previewer may still print with white lines. Always order a proof copy before wide distribution.

### Is a white edge on my proof a KDP defect or my file?

In most cases it is the file. White lines from trim tolerance are a normal print outcome when bleed is insufficient. The fix is in the source file, not a reprint request.

## Fix the File, Then Proof Again

White lines on a KDP cover are not random bad luck. They are a predictable consequence of specific file setup decisions — missing bleed, borders too close to trim, wrong export settings, or backgrounds that stop at the trim line. Every cause in this article has a direct fix.

Before uploading your corrected cover, run the PDF through [KDPPreflight](/tools/kdp-cover-checker) to verify bleed extension, safe-area placement, border risk, and export dimensions. Then order another proof copy before approving wide distribution.
